introduction_markdown:
This paper is arranged in three sections, A, B and C. Section A: answer ALL 5 questions; you will be graded for the best 4 answers. Section B: answer ALL 2 questions in this section using the spaces provided; both questions carry equal marks. Section C: answer ONLY TWO questions out of three; if you attempt more than 2 questions, only the first two will be considered. Where appropriate, equations and diagrams should be used to illustrate your answers. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators are allowed. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

**Useful data:** specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g$^{-1}$ $^\circ$C$^{-1}$; 1 faraday = 96000 coulombs; Avogadro number = $6.02\times10^{23}$; molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24000 cm$^3$.

A student carried out a series of laboratory tests on two unknown salts, **X**, **Y** and an organic compound **Z**, in order to determine their identities. Study the following table and complete the information required.

| No | PROCEDURE | OBSERVATION | INFERENCE OR CONCLUSION | Marks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a)i | To 2 cm$^3$ of compound **X** in a test tube is added dilute HCl(aq) | Colourless, odourless gas is evolved, which turns lime water milky | Identify the gas ........ Which anion is present in **X**? ........ | 2 marks |
| a)ii | Clean a graphite pencil with concentrated HCl. Pick up a bit of solid **X** on the pencil and introduce it in a blue Bunsen flame | Brick red flame colour | Which cation is present in **X**? ........ Using the ions in a(i) and a(ii) above, identify the compound **X** ........ | 2 marks |
| b)i | To 2 cm$^3$ of **Y** in a test tube, a few drops of aqueous sodium hydroxide are added | ........ (to be completed) | Cu$^{2+}$ ions are present in **Y** | 1 mark |
| b)ii | To 2 cm$^3$ of solution **Y** are added 2 cm$^3$ of BaCl$_2$(aq) followed by dilute HCl(aq) | White precipitate is observed. Precipitate is insoluble in excess acid | Identify the precipitate ........ Which anion is present in **Y**? ........ Identify the compound **Y**, using information from b(i) and b(ii) ........ | 3 marks |
| c)i | Liquid **Z** is tested with both red and blue litmus paper | No change in colour in each case | What can you say about liquid **Z**? | 1 mark |
| c)ii | To 2 cm3 of liquid compound **Z** is added a piece of sodium metal. | Effervescence occurs. The gas released burns with a 'pop' sound | Identify the gas evolved ........ Give the functional group in **Z** ........ | 2 marks |
| c)iii | Liquid **Z** is introduced to a Bunsen flame | Liquid burns with a pale blue flame | Suggest one substance that can be **Z** | 1 mark |

*(12 marks)*

questions.enonce_markdown:
Using tests a(i) and a(ii) of the table:

(i) Identify the gas, and state which anion is present in **X**. *[2 marks]*

(ii) State which cation is present in **X**, and, using the ions in a(i) and a(ii) above, identify the compound **X**. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The colourless, odourless gas that turns lime water milky is **carbon dioxide, $\mathrm{CO_2}$**. The anion present in X is the **carbonate ion, $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$**.

$$
\mathrm{CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2}
$$

(The gas turns lime water milky because of the formation of insoluble calcium carbonate: $\mathrm{CO_2 + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O}$.)

(ii) A **brick-red flame** shows the **calcium ion, $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$**. Combining the two ions, **X is calcium carbonate, $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Using tests b(i) and b(ii) of the table:

(i) Complete the observation column of test b(i). *[1 mark]*

(ii) Identify the precipitate, state which anion is present in **Y**, and identify the compound **Y** using information from b(i) and b(ii). *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Observation:** a **light (pale) blue precipitate** forms; it does not dissolve when a few more drops of sodium hydroxide are added (it dissolves only in excess ammonia solution, not in excess sodium hydroxide). This confirms $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$:

$$
\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2OH^- \rightarrow Cu(OH)_2}
$$

(ii) The white precipitate, insoluble in dilute hydrochloric acid, is **barium sulphate, $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$**:

$$
\mathrm{Ba^{2+} + SO_4^{2-} \rightarrow BaSO_4}
$$

The anion present in Y is the **sulphate ion, $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$**. With the cation $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ from b(i), **Y is copper(II) sulphate, $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Using tests c(i), c(ii) and c(iii) of the table:

(i) What can you say about liquid **Z**? *[1 mark]*

(ii) Identify the gas evolved, and give the functional group in **Z**. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Suggest one substance that can be **Z**. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Liquid Z does not change the colour of red or blue litmus paper: Z is **neutral** (neither acidic nor alkaline).

(ii) The gas that burns with a 'pop' is **hydrogen, $\mathrm{H_2}$**. Z reacts with sodium to give hydrogen, so it contains the **hydroxyl group, $-\mathrm{OH}$**: Z is an **alcohol**.

$$
2\mathrm{C_2H_5OH + 2Na \rightarrow 2C_2H_5ONa + H_2}
$$

(iii) **Ethanol, $\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}$** (it is neutral to litmus, reacts with sodium and burns with a pale blue flame). Methanol or propan-1-ol are also acceptable.

Figure 1 is a graph to show the volume of hydrogen gas collected by a student from the reaction between dilute hydrochloric acid and Magnesium ribbon.

![fig-1](gce-ol-chemistry-2025-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_6_fig_1.png)

(i) At what time did the reaction come to an end?

(ii) Determine the volume of gas produced after 3 minutes *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The reaction is $\mathrm{Mg + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_2 + H_2}$.

(i) The reaction ends when no more gas is produced, i.e. when the curve becomes **horizontal**. On the graph this happens at **7 minutes**. After that the volume stays constant at about $95\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.

(ii) Draw a vertical line from 3 minutes on the time axis up to the curve, then a horizontal line to the volume axis. The reading is about **52 $\mathrm{cm^3}$** of hydrogen (a value between 50 and 55 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ is acceptable).

questions.enonce_markdown:
A student is required to prepare and collect a dry sample of ammonia gas in the laboratory.

(i) State the reagents used ........ and ........

(ii) State the reaction condition.

(iii) Why is the ammonia collected by downward displacement of air? *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The reagents are **ammonium chloride** (or another ammonium salt such as ammonium sulphate) and **calcium hydroxide** (slaked lime), both solids, mixed together.

(ii) The mixture is **heated** (gently):

$$
\mathrm{2NH_4Cl + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow CaCl_2 + 2NH_3 + 2H_2O}
$$

Check: N 2 = 2; H 8 + 2 = 6 + 4; Cl 2 = 2; Ca 1 = 1; O 2 = 2. The gas is dried by passing it through a tube of **quicklime (calcium oxide)**; concentrated sulphuric acid and calcium chloride cannot be used because they react with ammonia.

(iii) Ammonia is **less dense than air** (relative molecular mass 17, against an average of about 29 for air), so it rises. It is collected in a gas jar held **upside down**, and the air is pushed out downwards, hence "downward displacement of air". It cannot be collected over water because it is **extremely soluble** in water, and a dry sample is required.
